tldr: Facet-0 is a robotic foundation model that simultaneously predicts and values actions and their resulting wrist wrenches. In PC assembly tasks requiring sub-millimeter tolerances of 0.1 to 0.3 mm, it achieved an average success rate of 82%—roughly 5.5x that of existing VLAs.
hero_caption: An overview of the precision PC assembly tasks tackled by Facet-0. Across five contact-rich tasks—GPU, RAM, hard disk, CPU, and CPU socket lever—it achieves precise assembly motions by considering contact forces in addition to vision-language instructions.
overview:
Recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models handle diverse tasks with great flexibility, but they often stumble on precision tasks like manufacturing assembly during the "final millimeter." When mating parts with sub-millimeter clearances, motions that look identical visually can lead to excessive friction or jamming from slight misalignments, causing the entire task to fail.

Prior works have fed force sensor readings into model inputs or paired policies with compliant control to yield against external forces. However, treating contact forces merely as "past observations" prevents policies from actively anticipating the physical consequences of their planned motions. This prompted the authors to explore a new approach: predict actions and their resulting forces as a joint pair, and value those physical consequences using reinforcement learning.

The proposed model, Facet-0, is trained on the force-synchronized ManuFacet-1K dataset to jointly generate executable actions and predicted wrist wrenches. Furthermore, an Action-Wrench Critic trained on deployment rollouts distinguishes beneficial contacts from dangerous jamming, while a lightweight bounded actor adapts quickly to novel parts.

Evaluated on five real-world PC assembly tasks, Facet-0 posted an impressive 82% success rate, whereas the strongest VLA baseline topped out at 15%. This study clearly highlights the importance of predicting and valuing contact in precision manipulation.
contributions: Built ManuFacet-1K, the first large-scale force-synchronized assembly corpus spanning roughly 1,000 hours across three robot embodiments and two PC chassis types
Proposed a unified semantic-contact representation that jointly predicts actions and resulting wrist wrenches (forces and moments), coupling task semantics with contact physics
Developed an Action-Wrench Critic that evaluates action-wrench pairs to reinforce beneficial contacts via RL, alongside a lightweight bounded actor for few-shot adaptation to novel parts
Demonstrated an 82% average success rate (5.5x the strongest baseline) with 50 ms command latency on precision PC assembly tasks with 0.10 to 0.30 mm clearances

sections.heading: Breaking the "Final Millimeter" Barrier: A Foundation Model That Predicts Contact
sections.summary: In precision assembly, tiny positioning errors cause excessive contact forces and jamming, yielding opposite outcomes from visually identical motions. This paper introduces Facet-0, modeling contact not just as an observation, but as a future physical consequence of action.
sections.details:
Modern VLA models show remarkable success following instructions in open-world settings, but they hit a wall in contact-rich, precision manufacturing tasks. Vision and language can guide parts near the target interface, but the real challenge lies in the precision contact of the "final millimeter." At clearances of just 0.1 mm, minor pose errors induce large lateral reaction forces, friction, and part jamming.

Traditional approaches have added force readings to inputs, stabilized contacts with compliant control, or refined policies using real-robot RL. Yet these methods treat contact as "past records" or "low-level feedback." They lack a framework to predict the causal relationship—what forces will occur if a certain action is taken—and evaluate whether those forces are good or bad.

Facet-0 rethinks this problem from the ground up. Combining a PaliGemma-based VLA with flow matching, it forms a unified representation that blends multi-view images, language instructions, kinematic states, and wrist-wrench history. Its defining feature is generating Cartesian action chunks simultaneously with the predicted wrenches they are expected to induce. Furthermore, deployment rollouts train a Critic on these action-wrench pairs to selectively reinforce safe, compliant contact behaviors.

sections.heading: How Does It Differ from Existing VLAs and Force Control?
sections.summary: This section reviews five research areas—VLA foundation models, force/tactile policies, classical contact control, learning from deployment, and manipulation datasets—clarifying the unique contributions of this work.
sections.details:
This work sits at the intersection of five major research trends:

- VLA Foundation Models: Recent VLAs like OpenVLA and $\pi_0$ achieve broad generalization by generating action chunks. However, their outputs are generally restricted to geometric motions (trajectories), ignoring contact forces. Facet-0 stays grounded in language instructions while including predicted wrenches directly in its output space alongside actions.

- Force/Tactile Policies: Works like ForceVLA and TA-VLA increasingly use 6-axis wrench data as inputs or auxiliary prediction targets. Yet most remain within the bounds of imitation learning. Facet-0 takes this further by directly scoring predicted wrenches using an RL Critic during deployment rollouts to guide policy improvement.

- Classical Contact Control: Hybrid position/force control and impedance control provide solid theory for stabilizing physical contact. Facet-0 does not replace them. Instead, it delegates roles: a compliant controller runs as the lowest execution layer at 200 Hz, while the higher-level learned policy predicts and plans contact outcomes.

- Learning from Deployment: Following methods like SERL and RECAP that learn value functions from real-robot rollouts, Facet-0's Action-Wrench Critic evaluates predicted forces alongside geometric task progress. This lets it tell the difference between smooth insertion and a jammed state forced into the same depth.

- Datasets: While datasets like Open X-Embodiment and DROID offer great diversity, they lack synchronized force readings and phase annotations for precision assembly. ManuFacet-1K fills this critical gap.

sections.heading: ManuFacet-1K: A 1,000-Hour Force-Synchronized Assembly Corpus
sections.summary: A roughly 1,000-hour, high-precision force-synchronized dataset collected across three robot types and two PC chassis styles. It features annotations across seven skill phases and 0.5 mm motion resolution.
sections.details:
Teaching models precision assembly demands data where images, actions, and wrist forces are synchronized down to the millisecond. Operating common-spec robotic cells across multiple centers, the authors compiled ManuFacet-1K, a corpus totaling approximately 1,000 hours.

- Corpus Composition (Section 3.1): The tasks cover four components: CPU (37.3%), RAM (21.9%), Disk (23.4%), and GPU (17.3%). Each cell includes a torque-controlled arm, a parallel gripper, a 6-axis wrist force-torque sensor, and three RGB cameras, teleoperated via haptic master devices. Each frame records a 13-dimensional state (wrist pose, gripper opening, 6-axis wrench) with a motion resolution of 0.5 mm.

- Skill Phase Taxonomy (Section 3.2): Tasks are split into seven phases: approach, align, insert, press, seat, fasten, and retreat. Five contact-involved phases are labeled "contact-critical." Although contact frames make up only a fraction of the total dataset, they hold most of the information determining task success or failure.

- Collection and Curation (Section 3.3): Data is cleaned through a high-quality pipeline involving strict timestamp-based multimodal synchronization, filtering of operator slips and sensor saturation, VLM-generated subtasks and instruction captions, and preservation of anomaly-recovery action pairs.

captions.F2: Breakdown of the ManuFacet-1K dataset, showing proportions, subtask distributions, and episode length statistics across the four main assembly tasks: CPU, RAM, Disk, and GPU.

sections.heading: An Architecture That Simultaneously Predicts Actions and Future Forces
sections.summary: Learn how the model forms a shared representation from vision, language, kinematics, and force history, and uses flow matching to jointly generate future action chunks and predicted wrenches.
sections.details:
Why should a policy predict wrenches instead of just "reading" them? Simply feeding current wrench readings only provides a backward-looking view of past actions. It fails to serve as an active learning signal for how to adjust upcoming motions. Facet-0 solves this by decoding executable actions and future wrenches together.

- Multimodal Integration (Section 4.1): At step $t$, the model takes three camera views, a text instruction $\ell$, the robot's kinematic state $s_t^{\mathrm{kin}} \in \mathbb{R}^7$ (pose and gripper state), and a recent wrench history $W_{t-K+1:t} \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times 6}$ over $K=10$ steps. A 10-step window is critical because a single-step reading cannot distinguish the onset of contact from steady-state friction. These streams are fused into a semantic-contact representation $h_t^c$.

- Joint Action-Wrench Flow Matching (Section 4.2): Conditioned on $h_t^c$, the model generates a joint proposal $Y_t = [A_{t:t+H-1}, \widehat{W}_{t+1:t+H}] \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times 13}$ over horizon $H=50$. Here, $A$ represents executable Cartesian action commands, while $\widehat{W}$ denotes the expected wrist wrenches resulting from those actions. Only $A$ is sent to the robot; $\widehat{W}$ is non-commanded. Training alternates between a conditional flow-matching loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AW}}$ on ground-truth $Y_t^{\mathrm{data}}$ and a VQA cross-entropy loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{VQA}}$ for task semantics.

- Coarse-to-Fine Decoding: By pairing a 5–10 Hz coarse global generator (Coarse Expert) with a 20 Hz refinement module (Refinement Expert) that updates trajectories near contact, the system achieves both fast inference and high precision.

captions.F3: Overall architecture of Facet-0: (a) constructs a joint representation from vision-language and wrench history, generating actions and wrenches across two coarse-to-fine stages; (b) uses structured attention masks to separate VQA from language-contact learning; (c) value-guided RL refinement; (d) lightweight bounded actor for local adaptation.

sections.heading: Valuing "Good Contact" Through Real-World Rollouts
sections.summary: Imitation learning alone cannot distinguish good contact from bad. Policies are refined using value evaluations from an Action-Wrench Critic, contact-selective credit assignment, and local adaptation for novel parts.
sections.details:
Policies trained solely on imitation learning can suggest reasonable actions, but they cannot assess "value"—which actions are safe and which risk jamming. To address this, the authors apply RL post-training using deployment rollouts.

- Contact Valuation (Section 5.1): A VLM judge determines subgoal completion $\Omega_t \in \{0, 1\}$ and contact phase $\varphi_t$. Step rewards are defined by combining phase success, elapsed time, and penalties for exceeding safe wrench envelopes. The Critic $Z_\psi(h_t^c, Y_t)$ takes in both the proposed action and the predicted wrench $\widehat{W}$ to predict return distributions. This allows it to assign clearly distinct values to a clean insertion versus a jammed state pushed to the same depth.

- Contact-Selective Credit (Section 5.2): If you naively reinforce frames with the highest returns, the policy over-indexes on free-space motions. Contact phases contain far fewer frames and show slower apparent visual progress. By setting separate score thresholds for free space and contact space, the policy applies a larger weight $\lambda$ selectively to frames that yield high value during contact.

- Local Policy Adaptation (Section 5.3): When part materials or tolerances change, high-level task semantics stay the same while local contact dynamics shift. Facet-0 freezes its large backbone and adds a lightweight local actor (just 6.6% of total parameters) that receives compressed tokens $z_t$, current states, wrenches, and reference actions from the frozen policy. Trained online via TD3+BC within a safe Cartesian bounding box $[a_{\min}, a_{\max}]$, it adapts quickly and safely to novel parts on the real robot.

captions.F4: Value curves of the Action-Wrench Critic during deployment. While a critic based only on images and poses (light curve) cannot distinguish subtle contact states, the critic evaluating both actions and predicted wrenches (dark curve) clearly separates successful insertions from visually identical jamming failures.

sections.heading: Validated on Real PC Assembly: A Dominant 82% Success Rate
sections.summary: Tested across five PC assembly tasks with 0.10 to 0.30 mm clearances, Facet-0 reached an average success rate of 82%, dramatically outperforming existing VLA baselines that topped out at 15%.
sections.details:
Experiments evaluated five assembly tasks on real PC chassis: RAM, GPU, Disk, CPU, and CPU LEVER. The tasks involve 23 distinct subgoals (9 free-space, 14 contact-critical) with tight clearances between 0.10 and 0.30 mm. Each task was tested over 20 single-attempt trials.

- Main Results and Ablations (Section 6.2): The full Facet-0 system achieved an 82% average success rate. In contrast, the strongest baseline, a $\pi_{0.5}$ + RECAP-style setup, reached only 15%. Standard $\pi_{0.5}$, force-input $\pi_{0.5}$+F, TA-VLA, and GR00T N1.7 all scored between 9% and 16%. Interestingly, all methods achieved 60–100% success on free-space picking, but baselines collapsed as soon as alignment and insertion began. Ablations showed that semantic-contact alignment alone reached 16%, adding RL post-training brought it to 38%, and adding local adaptation (Full) reached 82%, proving that all three components are essential.

- Impact of Post-Training (Section 6.3): In the Disk task compared against Advantage-Weighted Regression (AWR), Facet-0 with contact-selective credit boosted success rates from 20% to 65% and self-recovery rates from 44% to 81%. Concurrently, human intervention dropped by half, from 47% down to 24%.

- Transfer to Novel Parts (Section 6.4): When challenged with an unseen RAM module featuring different latch mechanics and stiffness, Facet-0 achieved a 45% success rate with just 10 demonstrations and 3 hours of on-robot adaptation (updating 6.6% of parameters), whereas baselines peaked at 5%. The policy naturally exhibited self-correcting retry behaviors, pulling back slightly upon detecting contact resistance to realign and press down again.

captions.F9: Adaptation behavior in the RAM insertion task. The left plot compares adaptation sample efficiency against baselines. The image sequence on the right illustrates an emergent retry behavior: when an initial angled contact risks jamming, the policy autonomously backs off, realigns, and seats the component properly.

sections.heading: Discussion and Future Outlook: A New Benchmark for Precision Manipulation
sections.summary: Facet-0 bridges the gap between VLA generalization and real-world contact precision by predicting and valuing wrench profiles. Future directions include multi-fingered hands and sensorless setups.
sections.details:
Facet-0 proves that robotic foundation models can meet demanding manufacturing tolerances by predicting the physical contact outcomes of planned actions, scoring their values, and adapting locally while preserving semantic task understanding.

This research offers an important lesson: simply feeding force sensor values as input tokens ("feeling contact") is not enough. The decisive factor is actively forecasting future contact and feeding back its quality via reinforcement learning ("acting on contact").

As noted in the paper's limitations, current evaluations focus on parallel-jaw grippers equipped with 6-axis wrist force-torque sensors on specific PC assembly fixtures. The authors suggest future avenues such as expanding to multi-fingered hands and applying force distillation to low-cost robot cells lacking wrist force sensors. With its dataset and training recipes open-sourced, this work marks a notable milestone in precision robotics.

sections.heading: Appendix: Control Hierarchy, Safety Operators, and Training Details
sections.summary: A look at the implementation details omitted from the main text, covering the 200 Hz compliant control hierarchy, safety operator design, and techniques for balancing flow matching and VQA during training.
sections.details:
The appendix details the engineering choices that keep Facet-0 safe and reliable on real robot hardware.

- Control Hierarchy (Appendix C): Action generation operates across three layers: a 5–10 Hz coarse global chunk, a 20 Hz refinement expert (around 0.5 mm resolution), and a 200 Hz compliant execution layer at the bottom. Predicted wrenches $\widehat{W}$ are used solely for representation learning and Critic evaluation; the lowest-level force control loop runs directly on measured sensor readings.

- Safety Operator $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{task}}$: Positioned between the policy and low-level controllers, this operator clamps per-step displacements. If the policy outputs an erratic target during early adaptation rollouts, this prevents the tool from lunging and structurally protects assembly fixtures from damage.

- Optimization Strategy (Appendix D): Because flow-matching MSE loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AW}}$ and VQA cross-entropy loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{VQA}}$ have very different scales and units, they are not simply summed. Instead, separate optimizers update them alternately in a 4:1 ratio. This allows the model to achieve high-precision action and wrench predictions without degrading language comprehension.

captions.F11: Training dynamics diagnostic plots: (a) shows that action-wrench branch loss converges equally well when co-trained with VQA as when trained alone; (b) shows the VQA cross-entropy loss decreasing smoothly, confirming that language understanding and physical prediction train together without interference.

takeaways: Force signals yield much richer representations when framed as predictable future physical consequences of actions, rather than just passive input observations.
By evaluating both proposed actions and predicted wrenches, a Critic can reliably separate clean insertions from visually indistinguishable jamming failures.

Freezing the expensive backbone to retain semantic knowledge while letting a lightweight local actor (a small fraction of total parameters) absorb contact dynamics provides a practical, safe path for real-robot adaptation.
limitations: Evaluations are limited to parallel-jaw grippers and specific PC assembly fixtures; applicability to dexterous multi-fingered hands or compliant deformable objects remains unverified.
The approach relies on 6-axis wrist force-torque sensors; deploying on low-cost commercial robot arms lacking force sensing will require additional techniques like force distillation.
While the task safety operator enforces kinematic limits like per-step displacement clamping, it does not provide strict theoretical passivity guarantees like energy tank methods.
